Application No. 241 of 1991 (Dhaka) 
Application No.1 of 1985 (Chittagong)
lawyer: AY Salehuzzaman, Deputy Attorney-General ------ For the Applicant.
parties:
Commissioner of Taxes, Chittagong (South) Zone, Chittagong ------ Applicant
vs
Mohammadi Trading Company ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The assessee in the instant case is a limited Company carrying on business under the name and style of Mohammadi Trading Company, which has subsequently been nationalised after the liberation of Bangladesh. 

 "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was legally justified in deleting the unpaid trading liability of Taka 25,68,022.00 under a section 10(2A)(iii) of the Income Tax Act holding that there was no cessation of business between the assesse and the parties in view of the unequivocal provisions of section 10(2A) of the Income Tax Act." 

 9. Section 10(2A)(iii) of the Income Tax, Act provided that "where for the purpose of computing profits or gains under this section, an allowance or deduction has been made in the assessment for any year in respect of any loss, expenditure or trading liability incurred by the assesse under clause (iii) such trading liability or a portion thereof has not been paid within three years of expiry of the previous year in which it was allowed; the amount received under clause (ii) or the value of benefit obtained under clause (ii) or so such of the portion of a trading liability as has not been paid under clause (iii) shall be deemed to be the profit or gains of business profession or vocation and to have accrued or arisen during the previous year referred to in clause (i) and clause (ii) or as the case may be, during the previous year immediately following the expiry of the years referred to in clause (iii) or a portion thereof is paid in a subsequent year, a deduction of such amount as has been paid shall be made in computing the profits and gains under this section in respect of that year." 

 11. In the instant case it appears that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes initially assessed by holding that on examining the balance sheet it appears that the liabilities were not paid within three years of their year of origin and hence liable to be added under section 10(2A) in total Taka 25,69,911.00 and it be done in exercise of the power under section 10(2A) (iii) of the Income Tax Act. 

 14. This fact is gathered from the ground of appeal before the Appellate Tribunal but it appears from the Judgment of the Appellate Tribunal that in course of hearing the authorized representative of the assesse argued quite a different set of arguments stating that the provision of section 10(2A) had no applicability in case under reference as there was practically no cessation of business transaction between the appellant and the parties concerned during the year 1972-73, 1973-74, 1974-75 and 1975-76 that as the same balances in respect of the liabilities for goods and expenses were carried from year to year till assessment year 1972-73 though the learned authorized representative's arguments regarding non-cessation of business and continuation of business transaction is of no basis. The Tribunal found that it is correct to say that transaction was going on between the appellant and its creditors and the appellant actually adjusted its account with the concerned creditors from year to year during the period after liberation and carried forward the closing balance on per normal accounting procedure. But while holding so, it did not at all take into account the credit balance in the accounts of the parties as they stood on 31.12.1971, where the assesse kept its pre-liberation debts at constant figures without any effect to the transactions as made during the year 1972-73 to 1975-76 which is after liberation period. The assesse contended that the appellant's concern was taken over by the Government on and from 16.12.72 and the appellant with a view to avoiding future problems and for facilitating accounting works separated the liabilities existing before 16.12.71 from the liabilities occurring after 16.12.71. The Tribunal found that the assesse in fact bifurcated its liabilities by turning it into pre-liberation and after-liberation liability and the Tribunal found that there were series of business transactions between the appellant and its creditors during the year 1972 to 1976. In that circumstances the credit cannot be-taken to be unpaid liabilities in isolation' from the transaction which took place between the parties over the years and the Tribunal found that the mischief of section 10(2A) is not applicable in a case like this where an assesse did not cease to have any further transaction with his creditors and the debt lies outstanding for more than three years. 

 17. From the time it arose the assesse may continue with his business with his creditors after the initial credit taken by non-payment for goods supplied and to be paid but without paying the previous amount, carry on business with the supplier would not mean that the original trading liability as in the instant case which accrued in the year 1971 would be merged with the subsequent trading balance of the assesse with his old supplier when in the books of account of the supplier and the assesse those trading liabilities are still shown to be in existence. It is further seen from the order of the Taxing authority that the said Assistant Commissioner of Taxes directed the authorized representative to submit before him the evidence regarding the date of origin of 'those liabilities and whether they were liquidated but the authorized representative could not submit any such evidence of the origin but he submitted confirmation letters from Al-Mustafa Industries Ltd., Hasni Vanaspati Manufacture Company Limited and Hasni Oil Mills in respect of these liabilities. In each of these letters it has been stated that as per their books of account as on 16.12.71 the amount under consideration was receivable from the appellant company and not yet paid. None of these letters specifically stated the actual date of origin of these liabilities but simply stated that the liabilities originated during the pre-liberation period. In such circumstances the Taxing authority considered that these liabilities originated during the accounting period ending on 31.12.71 corresponding to the financial year 1972-73 and as such the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes has correctly brought to tax under section 10 (2A) all the Trading liability amounting to Taka 22,68,022.00 during the assessment year 1976-77 and also the liability in respect of creditors for expenses amounting to Taka 21,889.00 to tax. 

 19. On a similar matter reported in 1977 BTD page 154 a Division Bench of this court consisting of K. Hossain and Badrul Haider Chowdhury JJ known as Baishaki Punji Tea Company Limited case, answered the question in the negative. 

 20. In. that case under report the assesse having business of manufacturing and sale of tea there was a question of inclusion and non-inclusion of "trading liability" to the extent of Taka 22,12,394.00 upto the accounting year 1962, the question was, can it include the assessment year 1961-1962. This amount has been added to the assessee's income under section 10(2A) (iii) of the Income Tax Act. Their Lordships answering the question in the negative held: that holding that the limitation is three years and it cannot be extended retrospectively any further and their Lordship's explanation of the law shows that this is a clear provision of law and the liability if not paid within three years it cannot be extended further as unpaid. 

 21. In this view of the matter our answer to the question is in the negative and we hold that the Appellate Tribunal was not correct in holding that in case there is no cessation of business with the outside supplier of credit which is the trading liability the mischief of section 10(2A) (iii) is not alternated. We hold that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes was correct in assessing tax under section 10(2A) (iii) and it was correctly upheld by the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes.
